title: Prototypes and Inheritance
summary: Property lookup falls through a chain of prototype objects, not a class hierarchy. `class` is sugar over exactly this mechanism — understanding the chain explains inheritance, shadowing, and a classic shared-state bug.

slides.markdown:
JavaScript doesn't have classes in the sense C++ or Java do. It has **objects linked to other objects**, and property lookup falls through that link when it can't find something locally. `class` syntax, which every modern codebase uses, is a thin layer of sugar over this exact mechanism.

That matters in interviews for a specific reason: candidates who only know `class` can name the vocabulary ("extends", "super") but can't explain *why* `instanceof` works, why methods live in one place instead of being copied per object, or why mutating a shared object on a prototype affects every instance.

This topic builds the prototype chain from the ground up, then shows exactly what `class` compiles down to — so both mental models collapse into one.

slides.subTitle: How property lookup falls through
slides.markdown:
Every object has an internal link to another object — its **prototype**. When you read a property, the engine checks the object itself first; if it's not there, it checks the prototype; if not there, the prototype's prototype; and so on, until it reaches `Object.prototype`, whose own prototype is `null`, ending the chain.

```javascript
const animal = { eats: true };
const rabbit = Object.create(animal); // rabbit's prototype is animal
rabbit.hops = true;

rabbit.hops; // true — own property
rabbit.eats; // true — found on animal, via the prototype link
rabbit.flies; // undefined — not found anywhere in the chain
```

`rabbit` doesn't **copy** `eats` from `animal` — it looks it up through the link, every time. If `animal.eats` changes later, every object chained to it sees the new value on their next lookup.

slides.subTitle: The naming confusion, resolved
slides.markdown:
Three different things share confusingly similar names — worth separating explicitly:

- **`obj.__proto__`** — a (legacy, but still widely supported) accessor for an *instance's* actual prototype link. `rabbit.__proto__ === animal`.
- **`Fn.prototype`** — a property that exists **only on functions**, holding the object that will become the prototype of anything created with `new Fn()`. It is not `Fn`'s own prototype.
- **`Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)`** — the modern, standard way to read an instance's prototype link. Prefer this over `__proto__` in real code; `__proto__` is a legacy accessor that some environments don't optimize as well.

The trap: `Fn.prototype` and `new Fn().__proto__` are the **same object** — `Fn.prototype` is the template, and every instance's internal link points at it. But `Fn.__proto__` (no `.prototype`) is something else entirely: it's `Function.prototype`, because `Fn` itself is an object too, an instance of `Function`.

slides.subTitle: No classes or constructors at all
Overriding and shadowing
slides.markdown:
Setting a property on an instance never changes the prototype — it creates (or overwrites) an **own** property that lookup finds before it ever walks the chain. This is called **shadowing**:

```javascript
const rex = new Dog("Rex");
rex.bark = function () { return "Rex is quiet today"; }; // own property
rex.bark(); // "Rex is quiet today" — own property wins
delete rex.bark;
rex.bark(); // "Rex says woof" — falls through to Dog.prototype again
```

`hasOwnProperty` (or `Object.hasOwn`) tells you which side of the chain a property came from — useful for distinguishing "this instance overrode the method" from "this instance is just using the shared one." `for...in` walks the whole chain including inherited enumerable properties, which is why real code almost always guards it with `hasOwnProperty` or uses `Object.keys` instead, which only returns own properties.

| | Classical (Java/C++ mental model) | Prototypal (JavaScript's actual model) |
|---|---|---|
| **What inherits** | a class, a static blueprint | an object, linked at runtime to another live object |
| **When the link is set** | fixed at compile time | can be changed at runtime with `Object.setPrototypeOf` |
| **Where methods live** | in the class definition | on a prototype object, itself just an object |
| **`extends`** | subclassing a blueprint | chaining one prototype object onto another |

`class`/`extends` deliberately borrows classical **vocabulary** to be approachable, but the underlying model is still live objects linked to live objects. The practical consequence: mutating `Dog.prototype` after instances already exist changes what those existing instances see on their next lookup — something impossible in a true compile-time class model, and a real (if rare) source of bugs when code monkey-patches a prototype.

slides.sectionTitle: Why prototype lookup is fast, mostly
slides.subTitle: Hidden classes and the senior nuance
slides.markdown:
Walking a chain on every property read sounds slow, but engines don't actually do a linear walk each time. V8 and similar engines track an object's **shape** (its "hidden class" — the set of property names and where they live in memory) and cache the result of a lookup against that shape, so repeated access to `rex.bark` after the first lookup is close to a direct memory read, not a chain traversal.

The catch: that optimization depends on objects sharing a **consistent shape**. Adding or deleting properties on an object after construction, or building objects with the same "logical" fields in different orders, forces the engine to create new hidden classes and can silently de-optimize hot code paths — the practical reason "always initialize all instance properties in the constructor, in the same order" is real production advice and not just a style preference.

When something "impossible" happens with inherited state — an instance seeing another instance's data, a method behaving differently after some unrelated code ran — the prototype chain is the first thing to suspect, in this order:

1. **Is the mutated thing an object/array, and is it declared on a prototype rather than in the constructor?** → shared-reference bug.
2. **Was a method reassigned on an instance, shadowing the prototype's version?** → check `hasOwnProperty`.
3. **Did something call `Object.setPrototypeOf` or reassign `Fn.prototype` after instances were already created?** → existing instances follow the live link and see the change immediately.

All three collapse to the same fact this whole topic has built toward: prototypes are **live, shared objects**, looked up on every access — never a static, per-instance copy.
